qa.question:
As noted in the chairman’s statement, Tong Guan Food Products Sdn. Bhd. recorded a 
1.6% decline in revenue to RM141.8 million, mainly due to lower sales of biscuits and 
cooking oil products. Swee Hin Chan Company Sdn. Berhad reported a 10.8% decline in 
revenue to RM82.6 million, primarily due to lower selling prices and sales volumes for starch 
products. The group also holds a 30% stake in United Malayan Flour (1996) Sdn. Bhd. (UMF), 
which is accounted for as an associate.  
 
Over the past five years, the group’s growth appears to have stagnated, with losses 
attributable to shareholders reported in the past four years and a shrinking shareholders’ 
equity base. 
 
(Source: company annual report; emphasis added) 
 
With the STI hitting new all-time highs in recent months, the company’s share price has 
steadily declined over the years and last traded at around $0.85 per share. According to SGX 
StockFacts, the price-to-book value ratio is approximately 0.4 times.  

(Source: https://investors.sgx.com/market/securities?code=K03&type=stocks&lang=en) 
 
(i) 
Can the executive directors articulate the company’s investment merits and 
the strategy for restoring sustainable growth and profitability? In addition, 
what are the group’s competitive advantages, and which specific growth 
opportunities does management intend to pursue over the next three to five 
years?  
 
(ii) 
How does management intend to communicate the group’s investment 
merits and growth strategy to the capital market and investors?  
 
The three executive directors on the board are Mr Chew Soo Lin, Mr Chew Kian Boon Daniel 
and Mr Chew Kian Hong Michael.  
 
(iii) 
How are their respective responsibilities and decision-making authority 
delineated? Is there any overlap in their executive roles, and who has 
ultimate accountability for the group's overall P&L performance and the 
delivery of its turnaround strategy? Are all three executive directors 
engaged on a full-time basis in managing the group's affairs, and what are 
their respective time commitments? 
 
(iv) 
Given the erosion of shareholders’ equity from $58.2 million to $54.3 
million, how does the board assess the group’s ability to generate adequate 
returns on its capital base? What measures are being taken to improve 
capital efficiency, and how does the board ensure that further capital is not 
allocated to businesses or activities that consistently fail to generate 
acceptable returns?

As noted in the chairman’s statement, Tong Guan Food Products Sdn. Bhd. recorded a 1.6% decline 
in revenue to RM141.8 million, mainly due to lower sales of biscuits and cooking oil products. Swee 
Hin Chan Company Sdn. Berhad reported a 10.8% decline in revenue to RM82.6 million, primarily 
due to lower selling prices and sales volumes for starch products. The group also holds a 30% 
stake in United Malayan Flour (1996) Sdn. Bhd. (UMF), which is accounted for as an associate. 
Over the past five years, the group’s growth appears to have stagnated, with losses attributable 
to shareholders reported in the past four years and a shrinking shareholders’ equity base. 
(Source: company annual report; emphasis added)  
With the STI hitting new all-time highs in recent months, the company’s share price has steadily 
declined over the years and last traded at around $0.85 per share. According to SGX StockFacts, 
the price-to-book value ratio is approximately 0.4 times. 

2 
(Source: https://investors.sgx.com/market/securities?code=K03&type=stocks&lang=en)
(i) Can the executive directors articulate the company’s investment merits and the 
strategy for restoring sustainable growth and profitability? In addition, what are 
the group’s competitive advantages, and which specific growth opportunities does 
management intend to pursue over the next three to five years? 
Company’s Response : 
The Executive Directors acknowledge the Group’s recent performance and the 
need to restore sustainable profitability and improve shareholder returns. 
In FY2026, Tong Guan Food Products Sdn. Bhd. (“TGF”) remained profitable 
despite lower revenue, while Swee Hin Chan Company Sdn. Berhad (“SHC”) 
returned to profitability. The Group’s investment merits include (1) TGF’s 
established FMCG distribution network in Sabah, (2) SHC’s longstanding 
expertise in food-ingredient distribution in Malaysia, (3) their extensive 
customer reach through established distribution networks and strong supplier 
and brand-principal relationships, and (4) the Group’s 30% interest in United 
Malayan Flour (1996) Sdn. Bhd. (“UMF”), which provides strategic exposure to 
markets for wheat flour, oats, pulses and cooking oil. 
Over the next three to five years, subject to market conditions and unforeseen 
developments, Management intends to focus on higher-margin products, 
improved product mix, wider distribution coverage, operating efficiency and 
new brand and distribution partnerships at TGF and SHC, with a view to 
supporting revenue growth while managing costs. At UMF, its management 
team will continue to focus on improving milling competitiveness, optimising 
supply-chain operations and pursuing targeted value-chain improvements to 
strengthen profitability, under the oversight of UMF’s Board. Federal Oats Mills 
Sdn. Bhd. (“FOM”), a subsidiary of UMF, invested in a beverage factory as part 
of its business diversification efforts, with opportunities to broaden its product 
offerings and enhance purchasing and distribution efficiencies.  

3 
The Board will assess complementary growth, M&A and strategic divestment 
opportunities against commercial prospects, funding needs, expected returns 
and their potential to improve capital efficiency or shareholder value. 
(ii) How does management intend to communicate the group’s investment merits and 
growth strategy to the capital market and investors? 
Company’s Response : 
The Company communicates its financial results and business developments 
through SGXNet announcements, annual reports, its corporate website and 
general meetings. Management will continue to use these channels to explain 
the Group’s businesses, strategic priorities and progress more clearly. 
The Company will review its investor-relations arrangements in light of the SGX-
ST requirements taking effect on 1 January 2027. Any additional investor 
briefings or engagement activities will be considered where appropriate. 
The three executive directors on the board are Mr Chew Soo Lin, Mr Chew Kian Boon Daniel and 
Mr Chew Kian Hong Michael. 
(iii) How are their respective responsibilities and decision-making authority 
delineated? Is there any overlap in their executive roles, and who has ultimate 
accountability for the group's overall P&L performance and the delivery of its 
turnaround strategy? Are all three executive directors engaged on a full-time basis 
in managing the group's affairs, and what are their respective time commitments? 
Company’s Response : 
Mr Chew Soo Lin, as Executive Chairman, leads the Board, facilitates its 
effectiveness and constructive discussions, guides the Group’s strategic 
direction and oversees Group-level financial performance and corporate 
governance. 
Mr Chew Kian Boon Daniel oversees the Company’s day-to-day operations, 
Group ESG matters and key raw-material procurement for UMF. 
Mr Chew Kian Hong Michael supports Group business development, while his 
principal executive responsibilities are as Managing Director of TGF and UMF. 
All three Executive Directors are engaged on a full-time basis in managing the 
Group’s affairs, with responsibilities reflecting their respective business and 
functional roles. Each is accountable for execution and performance within his 
assigned responsibilities. The Executive Chairman provides overarching 
strategic leadership and oversees Group financial performance, while major 
decisions remain subject to the relevant Board and entity-level approval 
processes. Financial, operational and technology-related risks are managed 
through the Group’s respective operating and functional teams, with oversight 
by the Board and Audit Committee.

how does the board ensure that further capital is not allocated to businesses or 
activities that consistently fail to generate acceptable returns?

qa.question:
During the year, the group ceased to account for SGProtein Pte. Ltd. (SGP) as an associate 
following the dilution of its shareholding from 21.03% to 19.96% and changes in board 
representation, resulting in the loss of significant influence.  
 
The dilution arose from an increase in SGP’s share capital following the conversion of share 
options and the issuance of new shares to a new investor. The increase in the number of 
shares issued was approximately 204,949, representing approximately 5.36% of the 
relevant share base. 
 
Prior to the reclassification, the group recognised a loss on deemed disposal of $(1,707,566), 
reducing the carrying amount of its investment in SGP from $2.4 million to $692,434. The 
investment was subsequently reclassified as a financial asset at fair value through profit or 
loss, with a carrying value of $100,000, and a further unrealised fair value loss of $(592,000) 
was recognised. 
 
 
(Source: company annual report) 
 
(i) 
Can the audit committee provide shareholders with greater clarity on the 
basis for determining the carrying value of $692,434 following the loss of 
significant influence, which resulted in a deemed disposal loss of $1,707,566 
from the previous carrying amount of $2.4 million? What valuation 
methodology, assumptions and inputs were used, and was an independent 
valuation obtained? 
 
(ii) 
At what valuation did the new investor subscribe for shares in SGP? Did the 
group have any pre-emptive or anti-dilution rights in relation to its SGP 
investment, and if so, on what basis did the board decide against making 
further investments into SGP? 

(iii) 
How was the current carrying value of $100,000, classified as a short-term 
unquoted equity investment (financial asset), determined, given the 
previous carrying value of $692,434 (as an associate)? What valuation 
methodology and assumptions were applied?  
 
On 28 August 2026, the company reached an agreement in principle with Mr Michael Chew, 
an executive director, in relation to the proposed disposal of its 804,013 shares in SGP. Under 
the proposed arrangement, Mr Michael Chew or another purchaser acceptable to the 
company would acquire the shares for a consideration of not less than $100,000. 
 
(iv) 
Given the proposed transaction involves an executive director, how has the 
board assessed the fairness of the proposed consideration and managed the 
potential conflict of interest? What independent safeguards have been put 
in place to ensure that the disposal is conducted on an arm’s-length basis 
and in the interests of the company and its shareholders?
qa.answer:
During the year, the group ceased to account for SGProtein Pte. Ltd. (SGP) as an associate following 
the dilution of its shareholding from 21.03% to 19.96% and changes in board representation, 
resulting in the loss of significant influence.
The dilution arose from an increase in SGP’s share capital following the conversion of share options 
and the issuance of new shares to a new investor. The increase in the number of shares issued 
was approximately 204,949, representing approximately 5.36% of the relevant share base. 
Prior to the reclassification, the group recognised a loss on deemed disposal of $(1,707,566), 
reducing the carrying amount of its investment in SGP from $2.4 million to $692,434. The 
investment was subsequently reclassified as a financial asset at fair value through profit or loss, 
with a carrying value of $100,000, and a further unrealised fair value loss of $(592,000) was 
recognized. 
(Source: company annual report) 
Company’s Response : 
The Board acknowledges that the decline in shareholders’ equity and the Group’s 
recent losses require improved returns on capital. The Board works with 
Management to improve profitability through procurement discipline, operating 
cost efficiency and working-capital management. 
Material investments, acquisitions and disposals are assessed with regard to 
financial performance, business prospects, funding requirements, expected 
returns, risks and alternative uses of capital, subject to the relevant approval 
processes. Major proposals at UMF, a 30%-owned associate, are evaluated 
through UMF’s own governance arrangements, including financial feasibility and 
projected 
investment 
returns. 
Underperforming 
investments 
may 
be 
restructured or disposed of to improve returns, where commercially justified.

5 
(i) 
Can the audit committee provide shareholders with greater clarity on the basis 
for determining the carrying value of $692,434 following the loss of significant 
influence, which resulted in a deemed disposal loss of $1,707,566 from the 
previous carrying amount of $2.4 million? What valuation methodology, 
assumptions and inputs were used, and was an independent valuation obtained? 
Company’s Response : 
The S$692,434 represented the Group’s equity-accounted carrying amount of 
its retained 19.96% interest in SGP at the date of reclassification, derived from 
the previous carrying amount after recognising SGP’s post-acquisition results 
and the effect of the relevant share issuances and dilution. 
At Company level, the investment had been carried at a cost of S$2.4 million. 
Its remeasurement to S$692,434 resulted in a Company-level deemed-disposal 
loss of S$1,707,566. 
At Group level, the carrying amount of S$902,420 as at 31 July 2025 was 
reduced by S$209,986, representing the Group’s share of SGP’s FY2026 losses, 
to S$692,434. As a cross-check, KGL’s 19.96% share of SGP’s NTA of 
S$3,579,672 based on SGP financial information dated 28 February 2026 was 
approximately S$714,503, about 3.2% above the carrying amount. 
No separate independent valuation was commissioned. The carrying amount 
was assessed by Management using SGP’s available financial information and 
the Group’s accounting records. 
(ii) 
At what valuation did the new investor subscribe for shares in SGP? Did the group 
have any pre-emptive or anti-dilution rights in relation to its SGP investment, and 
if so, on what basis did the board decide against making further investments into 
SGP? 
Company’s Response : 
The 99,404 shares issued to the new investor were subscribed for at 
approximately S$5.03 per share, for an aggregate consideration of 
approximately S$500,000, under SGP’s Series A funding arrangements. 
KGL held general pre-emptive rights under Clause 4 of SGP’s Shareholders’ 
Agreement. KGL and the relevant shareholders consented to or waived the 
applicable rights in connection with the relevant new investor and employee-
option issuances, subject to the terms of the Shareholders’ Agreement. No 
separate anti-dilution adjustment was applied to those issuances. 
KGL previously participated in SGP’s FY2025 fundraising by subscribing for 
179,013 shares for S$900,000, through cash payment and conversion of an 
existing shareholder loan. As disclosed in the FY2025 Annual Report, KGL’s 
interest declined in stages from 30.00% to 21.03% during FY2025. The further 
new-investor and employee-option issuances in FY2026 diluted KGL’s retained 
804,013 shares from approximately 21.03% to 19.96%. In deciding not to 
make an additional equity investment, the Board considered SGP’s performance 

6 
to date, its medium-term strategic plan and expected future funding 
requirements, KGL’s minority position and the Group’s capital priorities. 
iii) 
How was the current carrying value of $100,000, classified as a short-term 
unquoted equity investment (financial asset), determined, given the previous 
carrying value of $692,434 (as an associate)? What valuation methodology and 
assumptions were applied? 
Company’s Response : 
Upon the loss of significant influence over SGP, the Group ceased applying the 
equity method and reclassified its retained 19.96% interest as an unquoted 
equity investment measured at fair value through profit or loss under SFRS(I) 
9. The investment was classified as a short-term financial asset because the 
Board was pursuing its disposal and expected it to be realised within 12 
months. 
The S$100,000 carrying value as at 31 July 2026 was determined using a fair-
value approach. As disclosed in the FY2026 audited financial statements, the 
market-based assessment took into account SGP’s adjusted net tangible assets 
and KGL’s percentage shareholding. Management also considered SGP’s 
financial position, its funding requirements and the indicative market evidence 
available in assessing the value of KGL’s interest. The subsequent negotiated 
proposal for KGL’s entire shareholding was considered additional supporting 
evidence, to the extent that it reflected conditions existing as at 31 July 2026, 
although the agreement in principle was reached after that date. The 
S$100,000 consideration related to the shares; reimbursement of KGL’s 
shareholder loan and related interest was addressed separately. The resulting 
unrealised fair-value loss was S$592,434 against the previous carrying amount 
of S$692,434. 
As an additional downside consideration, the Board examined the potential 
effect of SGP’s proposed Rescue Financing Framework (the “Framework”). On 
the illustrative ownership basis of 19.86% used in that Framework, KGL’s 
interest could have fallen to approximately 0.3256% if it did not participate in 
further funding. At the Framework’s illustrative post-money valuation of 
S$610,000, that residual interest would have an indicative value of 
approximately S$1,986. This illustrated the potential further dilution and 
capital exposure if the Framework proceeded on its proposed terms without 
KGL’s participation. The figures were illustrative and did not represent a 
completed transaction or a separate valuation of KGL’s investment as at 31 July 
2026. The same material terms of the subsequent proposed disposal were 
offered to SGP’s eligible existing investor shareholders through the applicable 
right-of-first-refusal process, and no shareholder elected to acquire KGL’s 
shares. 

7 
On 28 August 2026, the company reached an agreement in principle with Mr Michael Chew, an 
executive director, in relation to the proposed disposal of its 804,013 shares in SGP. Under the 
proposed arrangement, Mr Michael Chew or another purchaser acceptable to the company would 
acquire the shares for a consideration of not less than $100,000. 
iv) 
Given the proposed transaction involves an executive director, how has the board 
assessed the fairness of the proposed consideration and managed the potential 
conflict of interest? What independent safeguards have been put in place to 
ensure that the disposal is conducted on an arm’s-length basis and in the 
interests of the company and its shareholders? 
Company’s Response : 
Mr Michael Chew disclosed his interest in the proposed disposal to the Board. 
He negotiated with KGL in his capacity as a prospective purchaser, but did not 
participate in the Independent Directors’ deliberations and decisions on behalf 
of KGL concerning the proposed disposal. 
The assessment was undertaken by the Independent Directors, who considered 
(1) SGP’s historical performance and expected future funding requirements, (2) 
the potential dilution and indicative residual value under the proposed 
Framework, (3) KGL’s financial exposure if it retained the investment, and (4) 
the terms available for an exit. They also considered the separate 
reimbursement of KGL’s S$148,927 shareholder loan and applicable interest, in 
addition to the S$100,000 consideration for KGL’s 804,013 shares. 
The Board did not rely solely on Mr Michael Chew’s offer. An earlier indicative 
expression of interest from an existing SGP shareholder was conditional upon 
KGL not participating in the proposed shareholder financing and did not provide 
definitive terms or transaction certainty. Mr Michael Chew subsequently made 
an offer to acquire KGL’s shareholding in SGP, and following further discussions 
and negotiations with the Independent Directors, the proposed consideration 
was increased to S$100,000. 
Pursuant to the right-of-first-refusal provisions in SGP’s Shareholders’ 
Agreement, KGL’s entire shareholding was offered to the eligible existing 
shareholders on the same material terms. No shareholder elected to acquire 
KGL’s shares. 
Having considered the above factors and the measures taken to manage Mr 
Michael Chew’s potential conflict of interest, the Independent Directors 
consider the proposed consideration commercially reasonable and the disposal 
to be in the interests of KGL and its shareholders, subject to the remaining 
applicable requirements

In the chairman’s statement, the board noted that no dividend had been recommended for FY2026, 
following the group’s loss for the year. In FY2025, the group paid a dividend of $0.01 per ordinary 
share. The board considers it prudent to reinvest in the business to strengthen its financial position 
and support future growth initiatives.
The group’s FY2026 loss was primarily attributable to the decline in the value of its investment in 
SGP. At the company level, dividends received from subsidiaries amounted to $1.16 million, with a 
further $0.34 million received from UMF.

8 
       (Source: company annual report) 
(i) 
What has been the total shareholder return over the past 5, 10, 15 years, and 
since 23 August 2007? Has the board reviewed the company’s long-term 
shareholder returns and how does the board assess the performance and value 
creation? 
Company’s Response : 
Based on historical closing prices and assuming reinvestment of dividends, 
KGL’s estimated cumulative total shareholder returns as at 11 November 2026 
were −37.2% over five years, −54.4% over ten years, −22.9% over 15 years 
and −34.3% since 23 August 2007. 
The Board has considered these historical shareholder returns and 
acknowledges that, despite dividends paid, long-term returns have been 
affected by the decline in KGL’s share price. The Board continues to consider 
the Group’s performance and capital allocation with a view to sustainable 
shareholder value creation, including improving profitability and returns on 
capital and, where 
commercially appropriate, restructuring, strategic 
divestments or complementary investment opportunities. 
At the company level, retained profits of $2.6 million have turned into an accumulated loss position 
of $(53,548) as at 31 July 2026. 
        (Source: company annual report; emphasis added) 

9 
(ii) 
Given the company’s persistent losses and the board’s intention to reinvest capital, 
how does the board assess the merits of retaining and deploying further capital 
rather than returning capital to shareholders? What financial and strategic criteria 
must investments meet before capital is committed? Has the current management 
team demonstrated a track record of value creation through the group's operations 
and investments? 
Company’s Response : 
In considering whether to retain or return capital, the Board takes into account 
the Group’s working-capital and liquidity requirements, existing financial 
commitments, dividend-paying capacity and cash-flow outlook, alongside 
financial performance, capital requirements and strategic priorities. 
Before committing capital, the Board considers an investment’s strategic fit, 
funding requirements, expected returns and principal risks. It also considers 
whether continuing support is justified and may limit further funding, 
restructure or divest where the prospects no longer support additional 
exposure. 
The Board recognises TGF’s continued profitability and SHC’s return to 
profitability in FY2026. However, the Group’s operating results and investment 
performance have not consistently translated into satisfactory Group-level 
returns or shareholder value. Management’s performance will continue to be 
assessed against sustained profitability, cash generation, returns on capital and 
its willingness to restructure or exit low-return investments where commercially 
justified. 
(iii) 
Has the board undertaken a formal assessment of the company's optimal capital 
structure and the level of cash required to fund its operating needs? 
Company’s Response : 
The Company has not undertaken a separate formal study of its optimal capital 
structure or adopted a fixed cash-balance or gearing target. Nevertheless, the 
Board reviews the Group’s liquidity and capital requirements through annual 
budgeting, cash-flow forecasting and ongoing assessment of working capital, 
capital expenditure and funding commitments, taking account of trading 
volumes, inventories, receivables, market conditions and potential business 
opportunities. 
The Group’s trading and distribution businesses require liquidity to fund 
inventories, receivables and operating obligations, which fluctuate with market 
conditions. The Board will continue to assess the balance between financial 
flexibility, capital efficiency and shareholder returns. 
(iv) 
With more than $4 million in fixed deposits and cash and bank balances, has the 
board deliberated on a capital reduction to right-size its balance sheet and to allow 
shareholders to make their own capital allocation decisions? 

10 
Company’s Response : 
At 31 July 2026, the Group held approximately S$4.16 million in fixed deposits, 
cash and bank balances, of which approximately S$2.97 million was held at 
Company level. The balance was held within operating subsidiaries to support 
working-capital and operational requirements. These amounts are not 
automatically surplus cash available for distribution, having regard to liabilities, 
financial commitments and funding needs. 
The Board previously discussed the possibility of returning surplus cash to 
shareholders as part of broader deliberations on capital allocation and strategic 
alternatives. Those discussions were preliminary; no specific method, amount or 
timetable for a capital return was approved. Any future proposal would take into 
account available liquidity, operating needs and applicable regulatory and 
shareholder-approval requirements.

On 16 January 2026, SGX RegCo issued a Regulator’s Column on forward guidance, in 
which the regulator strongly encouraged issuers to provide meaningful forward-looking 
disclosures. 
 
SGX RegCo noted that forward-looking information consistently ranks highly among the 
information sought by investors, including institutional investors and research analysts, 
particularly regarding anticipated earnings and management’s strategy for achieving those 
outcomes. The regulator also clarified that forward guidance does not require auditor sign-
off and that issuers are not expected to update guidance immediately for every change in 
circumstances. Issuers should nevertheless make timely announcements in accordance with 
existing listing rules relating to material information and price-sensitive developments. 
 
SGX RegCo also highlighted that forward guidance should be viewed as a means for 
companies to signal confidence, build credibility with investors, and potentially support 
long-term shareholder value, rather than as a compliance exercise. 
 
The Regulator’s Column can be accessed here: 
https://www.sgxgroup.com/media-centre/20260116-regulators-column-forward-
guidance-why-it-matters-and-how-get-it
